Art Awakening

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A Cape Town man is introducing art into the lives of children as a way of helping them build confidence and tap into their creativity.

Unique Selling Point:
Luc van der Walt believes art should be accessible to everyone. He's taking his art workshops into townships to show children that art materials are all around them. Using recycled materials to paint on, he turns discarded boxes into canvases. He shows them how to make paint and charcoal, and even paintbrushes. The creativity is extraordinary, yet many of the children he works with, have never been exposed to art.

Summary:
An art workshop in Masiphumelele, a township on the Cape Peninsula, is introducing art into the lives of some of the children living there. Luc van der Walt says he does not teach the children how to paint, and many of them are new to this world, yet many of them take to art so naturally. He says the old Masters describe children's art as playful, inspiring and brimming with imagination. The results of the children's artwork is beautiful, and Luc is now looking to partner with galleries to exhibit the art, sell the art and channel that money back into the community. Luc has experience using art as a tool for healing, in refugee camps in the Middle East and the Democratic Republic of Congo. He has brought those skills back to South Africa, and is using them in his workshops with children aged between six and twelve years old.

Further information:
Luc works closely with women who run soup kitchens.
We will also speak to Zeitz MOCAA, the museum of contemporary art, about children's art and its natural creativity, how it has inspired artists over decades and continues to do so.

Script:


VO 1 Zeitz Mocaa - a non profit public museum in Cape Town.

VO 2 Where the artworks of some of Africa’s most talented artists are on display.

VO 3 Despite it’s imposing architecture, it’s open to everyone - a place where art has the potential to be both transformative.. and healing.

UPSOUND Liesl Hartman / Zeitz Mocaa: The reality is that the artists who are in our museum currently, their stories are about the lives and experiences of ordinary people in some way or another.

VO 4 Liesl Hartman has been an art educator for over thirty years and believes art needs to be at the core of a learning experience for a child.

VO 5 And with the right training, can be used as a tool for therapy.

UPSOUND Liesl Hartman / Zeitz MOCAA: Trauma and difficult experiences that children have growing up are often hard to speak about. Giving them a vehicle through art helps children work through that. When children are dealing with trauma there’s also a part of them that needs to escape that reality.

CLAIRE: How far are we trying to introduce art not just as a form of expression but as a healing tool in many of our underprivileged communities?

UPSOUND Liesl Hartman: There is a lot of passion out there, in young people young artists, who want to give back who see children in those spaces. And want to create positive environments for them. But, I think we have a ways to go.

VO 6 From the very impressive surrounds of one of the greatest modern art museums to the more simplistic surrounds of an art studio in Cape Town, we meet such an artist..

NATSOUND “When I’m painting a shape, I try not to make it too symmetrical or too accurate, try and leave it a bit wonky and it gives it a nice sort of charm”.

VO 7 Luc van der Walt. He’s using his skills not only to further his own ambitions…but to make a difference in the lives of children.

UPSOUND Luc van der Walt / Artist: We are all creative in our lives. We were complimenting you on your beautiful dress, you’re an artist to do that, and that comes from when you’re a child when you’re playing, experimenting. Art is everywhere in life.

VO 8 He says many contemporary artists are drawn to the artwork of children for its playfulness. And that’s exactly what he brings into his own work.

VO 9 For him, making the materials he uses for his artworks is part of the creative process.

VO 10 And he’s sharing his skills - once a week, with volunteers from his non profit Flowers for Africa, a ritual unfolds in the Cape Town township, Masiphumelele.

NATSOUND

VO 11 With a group of children, he trawls the streets in search of art materials.

VO 12 They return to the home of Philiswa Mlahlo - three days a week she runs a soup kitchen from here.

VO 13 But, on Fridays, it becomes more than that - a makeshift art studio.

NATSOUND Who wants this box? Me

LINK Pablo Picasso, one of the most influential artists of the twentieth century once said every child is an artist, the problem is how to remain an artist as we grow up.

VO 14 It’s that raw, uninhibited creativity that we lose as we age.

NATSOUND Claire writing Carte Blanche with a star Luc: Great star. Claire: I can’t do much else.

NATSOUND 1 Frikking amazing
Claire and Luc “There’s a house there. This car is great”.
This is the police car and this is the police station.
CLAIRE Where is it going?
Clip 793 The police station

VO 15 Luc is not just exposing the children to art, he’s also teaching them how to make their own paint and charcoal.

NATSOUND Claire: So what are we trying to do with all the sticks in the pot?
Luc: We close lid, put on burner, it doesn’t turn to ash, it turns into charcoal paint.

VO 16 Making the paint is a physical part of the workshop that the children love.

NATSOUND “We have wood glue mixed with water. Helps it to bind the paint. Claire: Aha”

VO 17 Luc has travelled the world and worked with organisations using art as a way of connecting with children. In refugee camps, he saw firsthand how it boosted self-esteem, and gave them back some of their stolen childhood.

UPSOUND Luc van der Walt / Artist: I noticed the children in refugee camps are growing up very quickly. They have to. Because it’s a serious situation and there’s not much opportunity to play. We gave them this platform. It brings this playful energy to a very harsh atmosphere. Especially children’s work, it’s so charming. It really created a positive influence on the community. And I really thought that could have a very positive impact in my own country.

VO 18 For Philiswa, meeting Luc and introducing art into the lives of the children she feeds from her soup kitchen, has had a profoundly positive impact.

UPSOUND Philiswa Mlahlo / Living Hope Soup Kitchen: For the children of Masi, I can say this is new for them. In this community, children are exposed to crime. They don’t have sports fields to play.

VO 19 The reality is that life is about survival here.

UPSOUND Philiswa Mlahlo: The children at home they don’t get food. The parents of the children they are drinking the alcohol. When they come home, the parents are not there they are in the shebeen.

VO 20 But, at Luc’s workshops, they’re able to escape into an imaginary world.

VO 21 At the end of the workshop, each charcoal drawing is treated and preserved.

NATSOUND “We use hairspray and we fix it. Claire: You’re teaching me all the tricks How did you discover this. Luc: “This is from art school, like a poor art students trick. (Claire laughs)

VO 22 His dream is to exhibit the children’s art in galleries, sell it and channel the proceeds back into the soup kitchen. He organised for a local gallery to display the children’s work - to give them a taste of a real exhibition.

UPSOUND Luc van der Walt / Artist: Children can share their spirit with the world, and then they can give back to those children, and then they can have the nutrition they need. That’s why I’m working with soup kitchens.

VO 23 Perhaps in the not so distant future one of these children’s artworks could be exhibited in some of our most famous galleries.

LINK: The Zeitz Mocca is the largest museum of contemporary African art in the world. It has a cathedral like atmosphere and features both temporary exhibitions and a permanent collection.

VO 24 The work on display here is undoubtedly beautiful - but how accessible is it, for children across Cape Town?

CLAIRE: Are we doing enough to make museums less intimidating? How do we bridge that gap?

UPSOUND Liesl Hartman: That is something this museum takes very seriously. We have conversations about access. Who is this museum for? All our programmes we provide are for free, our commitment really to that accessibility, but there’s a lot of work to do.

VO 25 True to their word, the Zeitz Mocaa offered to fetch the children from Masiphumelele and bring them to the museum for a tour.

NATSOUND

VO 26 It’s a day they won’t forget.
